screens.title: Accessing Device Camera and Gallery
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn why mobile apps ask to use the camera and photo library, how to request and check permissions, and how to use the expo-image-picker A P I to capture a photo or choose one from the gallery. We will focus on practical steps that work across iOS and Android in an Expo workflow, including the two common functions for media: one to open the camera and one to open the image library. You will also see how to respond when the user cancels, how to access the returned image URI and metadata, and how to prepare that image for upload. Along the way I will point out platform-specific requirements such as the privacy strings needed in iOS Info. plist and the permissions that matter on Android. A concrete example will walk through a small component that requests permissions, launches the picker, and displays the selected image. Finally, we will cover common mistakes like assuming permissions are already granted and failing to check the canceled flag. By the end you should be able to let users set a profile picture or attach images to posts while handling errors and privacy correctly. Consider how you would describe why the app needs camera access to a user — that reason belongs in your privacy description.

screens.title: Why permissions matter
screens.narratorSegment: Permissions are the gateway that lets an app access sensitive device features like the camera and photo library. On both iOS and Android, the operating system requires explicit user consent before allowing this access. In practice this means your app should check current permission status, request permission when necessary, and provide a clear explanation for why the permission is needed. On iOS that explanation is a string you add to the Info. plist file such as a camera usage description. Without that string iOS will often crash the app when it first attempts to access the camera. On Android, the relevant permissions include camera and reading external storage; Expo handles many manifest entries for you, but you must still request runtime permission where necessary. A common misconception is assuming permissions are implicit or granted by default. Always design the flow so the user understands why you need access and handle the denial case gracefully: show a helpful message and provide a way to open settings. Example: when a profile photo feature is tapped, check permission, if not granted call the request function, and if denied show an explanatory alert with next steps. Key takeaway: permission handling is both a technical step and a user-experience moment; handle it clearly and test on real devices so you catch platform-specific behavior.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Why permissions matter
Definition

Permission is the explicit consent required by the operating system to access the camera or media library. It is enforced at runtime and often requires platform-specific configuration.

Concrete example

If a user taps "Set profile photo", you request camera permission. If denied, show an alert explaining why and offer to open settings.

Common misconception

Assuming permissions are granted by default will cause silent failures or crashes, especially on iOS without Info.plist entries.

Pro tip

Explain the reason for the permission in user-facing text, not only in the manifest, so users are more likely to grant it.

Platform notes
  • iOS: add NSCameraUsageDescription and NSPhotoLibraryUsageDescription to Info.plist with a user-facing reason.
  • Android: ensure camera and read storage permissions are declared and test on real devices or emulators.
Check flow
  1. Check current permission status.
  2. If not granted, call the request function.
  3. If granted, open camera or gallery. If denied, show guidance.

screens.title: expo-image-picker vs native APIs
screens.narratorSegment: expo-image-picker provides a unified JavaScript A P I that abstracts platform differences and reduces the amount of native configuration you must write. In an Expo-managed project it is the recommended choice because it integrates smoothly with the runtime and exposes launchCameraAsync and launchImageLibraryAsync functions that return structured results with assets including URIs and metadata. A common alternative in bare React Native projects is react-native-image-picker, which exposes similar functionality but requires more native linking and configuration. The key practical advantage here is simplicity: with expo-image-picker you install the package and call request permission and launch functions from JavaScript. A useful mental model is to treat expo-image-picker as a thin cross-platform adapter that handles platform-level details for you. An important contrast is platform configuration: even with expo-image-picker you still must provide Info. plist strings on iOS; the library simplifies runtime code but cannot replace privacy requirements. Example scenario: for a profile photo feature in Expo, install the package, requestMediaLibraryPermissionsAsync, then call launchImageLibraryAsync and check result. canceled before using the returned URI. Common mistakes include not handling canceled or assuming the returned URI is directly uploadable without conversion. Takeaway: expo-image-picker accelerates development in Expo, but you still own permission UX and upload preparation.

screens.title: Typical image-pick workflow
screens.narratorSegment: A reliable image-picking workflow follows a predictable sequence: check or request permission, launch the camera or image library, inspect the result for cancellation, then either display the image or prepare it for upload. First, call the appropriate permission request: requestCameraPermissionsAsync for the camera or requestMediaLibraryPermissionsAsync for the gallery. If the permission is not granted, inform the user and stop. If granted, call launchCameraAsync or launchImageLibraryAsync. These functions accept options like allowsEditing, aspect, and quality; for profile images choose aspect [1,1] to crop to a square. The returned promise resolves to an object; if the user cancels, the canceled flag is true and no assets should be processed. When assets are present, result. assets[0]. uri is the local URI. At this point you can set state to display the image in an Image component or convert the file for upload using FormData. A common misconception is to assume the picker throws on cancel; instead it returns a canceled flag, so check that property explicitly. Example: for a profile uploader, request permission, launchImageLibraryAsync with aspect [1,1], then set the image URI into state for display. Key takeaway: treat permissions and canceled as first-class cases in your flow.

Step-by-step
  1. Check current permission status.
  2. If needed, request permission with the correct function for camera or gallery.
  3. Launch camera or library with options like aspect and quality.
  4. When resolved, check result.canceled before using assets.

  • quality: lower values reduce upload size.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Code Walkthrough
Core snippet
{`import React, { useState } from 'react'; import { Button, Image, View, Platform, Alert, StyleSheet } from 'react-native'; import * as ImagePicker from 'expo-image-picker'; export default function ImagePickerComponent() { const [selectedImage, setSelectedImage] = useState(null); const pickImage = async () => { if (Platform.OS !== 'web') { const { status } = await ImagePicker.requestMediaLibraryPermissionsAsync(); if (status !== 'granted') { Alert.alert('Permission Denied', 'Sorry, we need camera roll permissions to make this work!'); return; } } let result = await ImagePicker.launchImageLibraryAsync({ mediaTypes: ImagePicker.MediaTypeOptions.Images, allowsEditing: true, aspect: [4, 3], quality: 1, }); if (!result.canceled) { setSelectedImage(result.assets[0].uri); } else { Alert.alert('Image Selection Cancelled', 'No image was selected.'); } }; // takePhoto omitted here for brevity } `}
Explanation
  • Request permission explicitly and stop when not granted.
  • Use launchImageLibraryAsync with options for editing, aspect, and quality.
  • Check result.canceled before accessing assets array.
Try this

Change aspect to [1,1] and quality to 0.7 to adapt the same component for a profile picture flow.

screens.title: Understanding the result object
screens.narratorSegment: When you call launchCameraAsync or launchImageLibraryAsync the promise resolves to a result object that contains the essential data about the user action. The fields to rely on are assets and canceled. If the user completed the action, assets is an array where each item contains fields such as uri, width, height, and sometimes base64 if requested. The canceled flag is true when the user dismissed the picker without selecting or capturing an image. A frequent beginner mistake is assuming the function throws on cancel or that it always returns a single uri at the root of the result; instead check canceled and then read result. assets[0]. uri. Another detail is that URIs are typically local file URIs; on Android they may look like file:/// paths and on iOS you may see ph:// style references for assets. If you need to upload, you must convert the local file into a FormData entry or use a file-system A P I to read it. Example: after a successful pick setSelectedImage(result. assets[0]. uri) to display it in an Image component. Takeaway: treat the result object as the source of truth and guard every access with a canceled check to avoid runtime errors.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Result object
Key fields
  • canceled: boolean indicating user cancellation.
  • assets: array of selected assets, each with uri, width, height, and optional base64.
Common pitfall

Accessing result.assets[0] without checking canceled leads to undefined errors when the user cancels.

URI considerations

URIs are local file references. To upload, place the file into FormData or read the file contents using a file-system API if needed.

Example

After successful pick: setSelectedImage(result.assets[0].uri) and render with Image source={{ uri: selectedUri }}.

screens.title: Preparing an image for upload
screens.narratorSegment: Uploading a local image URI to a backend typically requires packaging the file into a multipart FormData object. The usual steps are: create a new FormData instance, append an object describing the file with keys for uri, name, and type, then send the FormData as the request body using fetch or axios. For example, append('image', { uri: imageUri, name: 'photo. jpg', type: 'image/jpeg' }). Some environments set the Content-Type multipart boundary automatically when FormData is used, so avoid manually overriding it unless required. The chapter example lists these steps clearly and demonstrates using fetch to POST the form. A common source of bugs is forgetting to set a name or type, which some servers depend on to infer file metadata. Another consideration is size: large images slow uploads and cost bandwidth. Use the quality option in launch... Async to reduce size or perform client-side resizing before upload. Finally, never upload images without explicit user consent and always secure the upload endpoint with authentication. Example workflow: after picking and checking canceled, create FormData, append the file, then POST to your upload endpoint. Takeaway: FormData is the standard client-side packaging approach; ensure name and type are present and prefer smaller images when possible.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Preparing for upload
FormData pattern
{`const formData = new FormData();
formData.append('image', {
  uri: imageUri,
  name: 'photo.jpg',
  type: 'image/jpeg',
});

const response = await fetch('YOUR_UPLOAD_URL', {
  method: 'POST',
  body: formData,
});`}
Practical notes
  • Include a sensible file name and MIME type when appending.
  • Let fetch/axios handle the multipart boundary header.
  • Consider resizing before upload to save bandwidth.
Pitfall

Sending raw uri string instead of FormData typically fails server-side file handling.

screens.title: Camera vs Gallery UX decisions
screens.narratorSegment: Deciding whether to open the camera or the gallery is both a UX and a technical decision. Use the camera when the user intends to capture a new photo in the moment, such as taking a quick selfie for a profile or scanning a document. Open the gallery when the user is more likely to select an existing image. From a code perspective, launchCameraAsync and launchImageLibraryAsync are symmetrical; both accept options for allowsEditing, aspect, and quality. For profile pictures, ask for square cropping with aspect [1,1] and allowsEditing true. For posts where wide images are preferred, choose aspect [4,3] or do not set aspect to let users crop freely. Consider the user's context: if the app needs immediate metadata like live location or timestamps, capturing a new photo is appropriate. A common misconception is thinking that allowsEditing always produces the same crop UI on every device; editing UIs can vary across platforms. Test both flows on iOS and Android to ensure the editing affordance matches your expectations. Example: provide two clear choices labeled "Take Photo" and "Choose from Gallery" and handle both permission flows similarly. Takeaway: match the picker mode and options to the user's intent and test editing behavior on target platforms.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Camera vs Gallery
When to use camera

For capturing new content now: selfies, document scans, or moment-based photos.

Example

"Take Photo" button opens the camera and requests camera permission before launching.

When to use gallery

For selecting previously taken photos or images saved on the device.

Example

"Choose from Gallery" opens the image library and requests media permissions when needed.

Editing options

Consider allowsEditing and aspect options to guide user cropping. Editing UIs vary by platform; test behavior on both iOS and Android.

screens.title: Integrating the picker into app state
screens.narratorSegment: Integrating image selection into your app requires thinking about state and lifecycle. Keep the selected image URI in component state or a higher-level store if multiple screens need it. When displaying a chosen image, pass the URI to the Image component's source prop. Be mindful of component unmounting during asynchronous operations: if a permission request or launch is pending and the component unmounts, avoid setting state afterwards to prevent warnings. Use a mounted flag or cancellation pattern if you anticipate rapid navigation. When showing large images, provide a placeholder spinner or low-resolution preview while processing. For multiple-image flows, maintain an array of asset objects rather than single URIs. Also consider where you store images long-term: local cache directories vs persistent storage, and whether you need to upload immediately or on a background task. A common misconception is storing binary data directly in state; prefer references (URIs) and use file-system APIs to perform heavy operations. Example: for a profile uploader keep profileImageUri in local state, show a circular image with border radius, and only upload when the user confirms. Takeaway: manage URIs as references, avoid heavy binary loads in memory, and guard asynchronous updates with lifecycle checks.

State patterns
  • Keep selected image URI in state as a string reference.
  • For galleries, store an array of asset objects.
  • Avoid storing large binary blobs in React state.
Lifecycle safety

Use a mounted flag to avoid setState after unmount when async permission or picker calls complete.

UX tip

Show a placeholder or spinner while image is being processed to communicate work in progress.

Example

Keep profileImageUri in state, render a circular Image when present, and upload only after the user confirms to avoid unexpected network calls.

screens.title: Privacy, consent, and storage
screens.narratorSegment: Privacy and consent are non-negotiable when handling user images. Always obtain explicit consent before uploading images to a remote server. If an image could contain sensitive information, consider additional protections such as encryption at rest, access controls, or avoiding server storage altogether. The lesson source reminds us to never upload user images without permission and to comply with applicable privacy regulations, so build a clear consent flow and explain what you will do with the image. From a technical angle, minimize the number of times an image is transmitted and store only what you need. When processing many user images, be mindful of memory usage in the client; use thumbnails for display and process the full-size image only when required. A common mistake is assuming local URIs equal persistent copies; local file paths can be ephemeral, and you should copy or upload explicitly if you need server storage. Example practice: show a confirmation dialog before uploading and indicate where the image will be stored and for how long. Takeaway: treat user images as sensitive data, get clear consent, and design your upload and storage strategy to minimize risk.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Privacy & Consent
Consent patterns

Ask explicit permission before uploading. Explain why you need the image and how it will be used.

Example

Show a confirmation that the image will be uploaded to update the profile and include a cancel option.

Storage & security

If storing images server-side, apply access controls and minimize retention. Consider encryption when appropriate.

Key Takeaway

Treat images as sensitive data: get consent, minimize uploads, and secure storage.

Operational tip

Provide a way for users to remove or replace images and document your retention policy in-app or in privacy settings.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Profile Picture Uploader
Starter checklist
  1. Run npx expo install expo-image-picker.
  2. Copy the starter component into App.js or a new file.
  3. Implement permission requests and handle denied status with alerts.
  4. Use aspect [1,1] and quality 0.7 for profile uploads.
  5. Display the selected image in a circular Image component.
  6. Package the image into FormData with uri, name, and type to upload.
Starter code snippet
{`// See starter code in chapter source. Key parts:
await ImagePicker.requestCameraPermissionsAsync()
await ImagePicker.launchCameraAsync({ allowsEditing: true, aspect: [1,1], quality: 0.7 })
if (!result.canceled) setProfileImage(result.assets[0].uri)
// Build FormData and POST for upload`}
Success check

You can see the selected image in the circular preview and the upload function sends FormData with the image file.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn why mobile apps ask to use the camera and photo library, how to request and check permissions, and how to use the expo-image-picker A P I to capture a photo or choose one from the gallery. We will focus on practical steps that work across iOS and Android in an Expo workflow, including the two common functions for media: one to open the camera and one to open the image library. You will also see how to respond when the user cancels, how to access the returned image URI and metadata, and how to prepare that image for upload. Along the way I will point out platform-specific requirements such as the privacy strings needed in iOS Info. plist and the permissions that matter on Android. A concrete example will walk through a small component that requests permissions, launches the picker, and displays the selected image. Finally, we will cover common mistakes like assuming permissions are already granted and failing to check the canceled flag. By the end you should be able to let users set a profile picture or attach images to posts while handling errors and privacy correctly. Consider how you would describe why the app needs camera access to a user — that reason belongs in your privacy description.

By the end of this lesson you will understand the permission model for camera and gallery access, be able to request permissions on both iOS and Android, and implement a simple image picker workflow using expo-image-picker. You will practice asking for camera and media library permissions, handle the responses that can be granted or denied, and learn to show a user-friendly message when access is denied. You will also know how to call the two primary functions that let users capture a new photo or pick an existing one, how to check for cancellation, and how to read the URI and metadata returned by the picker. Each objective focuses on a practical skill: requesting permission safely, launching the picker, showing selected images in the UI, and handling errors. These are everyday tasks for mobile apps that let users upload profile pictures or share photos. A concrete example in the lessons will walk you through a small component that requests permissions, launches the picker, and displays the selected image. Keep in mind that platform-specific setup is required, especially on iOS where privacy descriptions must be declared.

These additional objectives focus on practical behaviors and safety: you will learn to gracefully handle permission denial and user cancellations, to manage image size and quality when sending media, and to follow privacy-minded practices when storing or transmitting images. Graceful handling means showing a clear message to the user and not attempting to access the camera without permission. Managing size includes setting quality options and being prepared to resize or compress images before upload to reduce bandwidth. Safety practices include asking for consent before uploading images and being aware that URIs can point to local files that may need conversion before network transfer. Each objective pairs with a small hands-on task during the lab so you practice both the UI flow and the network preparation. These are essential skills for building robust, privacy-aware photo features in mobile apps. Think about what feedback you would show a user when permission is denied, and how you would let them change that decision later.

Permissions are the gateway that lets an app access sensitive device features like the camera and photo library. On both iOS and Android, the operating system requires explicit user consent before allowing this access. In practice this means your app should check current permission status, request permission when necessary, and provide a clear explanation for why the permission is needed. On iOS that explanation is a string you add to the Info. plist file such as a camera usage description. Without that string iOS will often crash the app when it first attempts to access the camera. On Android, the relevant permissions include camera and reading external storage; Expo handles many manifest entries for you, but you must still request runtime permission where necessary. A common misconception is assuming permissions are implicit or granted by default. Always design the flow so the user understands why you need access and handle the denial case gracefully: show a helpful message and provide a way to open settings. Example: when a profile photo feature is tapped, check permission, if not granted call the request function, and if denied show an explanatory alert with next steps. Key takeaway: permission handling is both a technical step and a user-experience moment; handle it clearly and test on real devices so you catch platform-specific behavior.

expo-image-picker provides a unified JavaScript A P I that abstracts platform differences and reduces the amount of native configuration you must write. In an Expo-managed project it is the recommended choice because it integrates smoothly with the runtime and exposes launchCameraAsync and launchImageLibraryAsync functions that return structured results with assets including URIs and metadata. A common alternative in bare React Native projects is react-native-image-picker, which exposes similar functionality but requires more native linking and configuration. The key practical advantage here is simplicity: with expo-image-picker you install the package and call request permission and launch functions from JavaScript. A useful mental model is to treat expo-image-picker as a thin cross-platform adapter that handles platform-level details for you. An important contrast is platform configuration: even with expo-image-picker you still must provide Info. plist strings on iOS; the library simplifies runtime code but cannot replace privacy requirements. Example scenario: for a profile photo feature in Expo, install the package, requestMediaLibraryPermissionsAsync, then call launchImageLibraryAsync and check result. canceled before using the returned URI. Common mistakes include not handling canceled or assuming the returned URI is directly uploadable without conversion. Takeaway: expo-image-picker accelerates development in Expo, but you still own permission UX and upload preparation.

A reliable image-picking workflow follows a predictable sequence: check or request permission, launch the camera or image library, inspect the result for cancellation, then either display the image or prepare it for upload. First, call the appropriate permission request: requestCameraPermissionsAsync for the camera or requestMediaLibraryPermissionsAsync for the gallery. If the permission is not granted, inform the user and stop. If granted, call launchCameraAsync or launchImageLibraryAsync. These functions accept options like allowsEditing, aspect, and quality; for profile images choose aspect [1,1] to crop to a square. The returned promise resolves to an object; if the user cancels, the canceled flag is true and no assets should be processed. When assets are present, result. assets[0]. uri is the local URI. At this point you can set state to display the image in an Image component or convert the file for upload using FormData. A common misconception is to assume the picker throws on cancel; instead it returns a canceled flag, so check that property explicitly. Example: for a profile uploader, request permission, launchImageLibraryAsync with aspect [1,1], then set the image URI into state for display. Key takeaway: treat permissions and canceled as first-class cases in your flow.

Let's walk through a small example component that demonstrates the full flow: requesting permissions, launching the picker or camera, checking the canceled flag, and displaying the resulting image. The component keeps the selected image URI in state. It first requests the correct permission depending on the action: media library for picking or camera for taking a photo. After ensuring permission is granted, it calls the appropriate launch function with options such as allowsEditing, aspect, and quality. The result returned by the picker contains an assets array; we use result. assets[0]. uri when canceled is false. You will see in the code how to alert the user when permission is denied and how to handle the cancelled case by showing an alert or a friendly message. A common misconception is to skip the permission check and rely on the picker to request permission implicitly. Explicit permission handling gives you control over UX and error messages. Try modifying the aspect to [1,1] for profile images or quality to 0.7 to balance size and appearance. After this walkthrough, you should be able to adapt the snippet to a profile uploader or a post-attachment feature.

When you call launchCameraAsync or launchImageLibraryAsync the promise resolves to a result object that contains the essential data about the user action. The fields to rely on are assets and canceled. If the user completed the action, assets is an array where each item contains fields such as uri, width, height, and sometimes base64 if requested. The canceled flag is true when the user dismissed the picker without selecting or capturing an image. A frequent beginner mistake is assuming the function throws on cancel or that it always returns a single uri at the root of the result; instead check canceled and then read result. assets[0]. uri. Another detail is that URIs are typically local file URIs; on Android they may look like file:/// paths and on iOS you may see ph:// style references for assets. If you need to upload, you must convert the local file into a FormData entry or use a file-system A P I to read it. Example: after a successful pick setSelectedImage(result. assets[0]. uri) to display it in an Image component. Takeaway: treat the result object as the source of truth and guard every access with a canceled check to avoid runtime errors.

Uploading a local image URI to a backend typically requires packaging the file into a multipart FormData object. The usual steps are: create a new FormData instance, append an object describing the file with keys for uri, name, and type, then send the FormData as the request body using fetch or axios. For example, append('image', { uri: imageUri, name: 'photo. jpg', type: 'image/jpeg' }). Some environments set the Content-Type multipart boundary automatically when FormData is used, so avoid manually overriding it unless required. The chapter example lists these steps clearly and demonstrates using fetch to POST the form. A common source of bugs is forgetting to set a name or type, which some servers depend on to infer file metadata. Another consideration is size: large images slow uploads and cost bandwidth. Use the quality option in launch... Async to reduce size or perform client-side resizing before upload. Finally, never upload images without explicit user consent and always secure the upload endpoint with authentication. Example workflow: after picking and checking canceled, create FormData, append the file, then POST to your upload endpoint. Takeaway: FormData is the standard client-side packaging approach; ensure name and type are present and prefer smaller images when possible.

Deciding whether to open the camera or the gallery is both a UX and a technical decision. Use the camera when the user intends to capture a new photo in the moment, such as taking a quick selfie for a profile or scanning a document.
